steps.title: Conditional probability
steps.idea: Knowing that $B$ happened shrinks the space of outcomes to $B$. The probability of $A$ given $B$ is the share of $B$ taken by $AB$.
steps.example: $n$ equally likely points, $k$ of them in $B$, $r$ in $AB$: $P(A \mid B) = \dfrac{r}{k} = \dfrac{r/n}{k/n}$.
steps.notes: Formula (6) is a definition, not a theorem. Station check (seed 202, 4000 points): $P(A \mid B) = 0.4$ exact, frequency 0.4110.

experiment.label: Condition on B in the Conditional probability station

steps.title: Multiplication theorem
steps.idea: Rewriting (6) gives the probability of both events through a condition; it also holds when $P(B) = 0$.
steps.example: Two cards from a 36-card deck: $P(\text{both aces}) = \dfrac{4}{36} \cdot \dfrac{3}{35} = \dfrac{1}{105}$.

steps.title: Independence, pairwise and mutual
steps.idea: $A$ does not depend on $B$ when the condition changes nothing; by (7) this is the product rule of lecture 1. Events are mutually independent when the product rule holds for every subfamily. Pairwise independence is not enough (Bernstein's example).
formula: P(AB) = P(A)P(B), \quad P(AC) = P(A)P(C), \quad P(BC) = P(B)P(C)
steps.example: A tetrahedron with faces red, green, blue and one face in all three colours. Each colour shows with probability $1/2$, each pair with $1/4$, all three also with $1/4$.
steps.notes: The lecture only names the example; the tetrahedron is Bernstein's own. Station check (seed 1928, 4000 throws): pairwise yes, mutual no; $P(ABC) = 0.25$ exact, frequency 0.2575.

steps.title: Total probability
steps.idea: Split $A$ by pairwise disjoint hypotheses $B_1, \ldots, B_n$ such that $A$ happens together with exactly one of them, and add up the paths that lead to $A$.
steps.notes: The hypotheses need not form a complete group; it is enough that their union contains $A$. When they do, $\sum_k P(B_k) = 1$ is a useful check. Station check (seed 118, 4000 particles): $P(A) = 0.43$ exact, share 0.4188.

experiment.label: Watch the particles in the Bayes tree

steps.title: An even face, two ways
steps.idea: A fair die. Formula (9) gives the same answer for different choices of hypotheses, as long as they cover $A$.
steps.example: Way 1: $B_2, B_4, B_6$ are the faces 2, 4, 6 (their probabilities add up to $1/2$, not 1). Way 2: $B_2 = \{2\}$, $B_4 = \{4\}$, $B_6 = \{1, 3, 5, 6\}$, a complete group.

steps.title: Bayes formula
steps.idea: After $A$ is observed, the prior weights of the hypotheses are replaced by posterior ones: each path to $A$ divided by all of them.
formula: P(B_k \mid A) = \dfrac{P(B_k)\, P(A \mid B_k)}{\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} P(B_i)\, P(A \mid B_i)}, \qquad k = 1, \ldots, n \qquad (10)
steps.example: Priors $0.5, 0.3, 0.2$ and likelihoods $0.02, 0.05, 0.1$: $P(A) = 0.045$, posteriors $2/9, 1/3, 4/9$. The least likely hypothesis a priori becomes the most likely.
steps.notes: Station check (seed 1763, 4000 trials): $P(B_3 \mid A) = 0.4444$ exact, observed 0.4351; posteriors sum to 1.

steps.title: The guessing student
steps.idea: A student solves the problem with probability $p$; otherwise picks one of 5 answers at random. Given a correct answer, how likely is it that it was a guess?
steps.example: $p = 0.6$: $\dfrac{0.4}{3.4} \approx 0.1176$. The lecture derives $\dfrac{1-p}{4p+1}$ correctly but prints $\dfrac{p}{4p+1}$ in the last line: a typo.
steps.notes: Checks: $p = 0$ gives 1 (always a guess), $p = 1$ gives 0. Station check (seed 7, 4000 students): exact 0.1176, observed 0.1148.

steps.title: Check yourself
steps.example:
1. $P(A) = 0.5$, $P(B) = 0.4$, $P(AB) = 0.1$. Find $P(A \mid B)$; are $A$ and $B$ independent?
2. Two urns: the first has 2 white and 3 black balls, the second 4 white and 1 black. An urn is chosen by a coin toss and a ball is drawn. Find $P(\text{white})$.
3. In question 2 the ball is white. Which urn is more likely now?
